newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-Palestinians struggle to clinch Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel-Palestinians struggle to clinch Hebron deal.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian negotiators continued to struggle on Thursday to clinch a deal that would clear the way for Israel to hand over most of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian rule.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said special Middle East envoy Dennis Ross believed the sides would need more than two days to wrap up an accord. A senior U.S. official said: "We think they probably have a week to go."

Talks between the sides resumed on Thursday evening in Jerusalem to hammer out an agreement for Israel to hand over 80 percent of Hebron to Palestinian self-rule. Some 400 Jews live in the heart of the city of about 100,000 Arabs.
"I really hope that there will be progress. The time has arrived that we conclude the protocol for implementing the interim agreement," said Israel's chief negotiator Dan Shomron.
Asked whether Ross's decision not to return to mediate the talks in Israel was a sign no deal was imminent, Shomron told Israel Channel One television: "I don't think that is a real signal."
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu scrapped a U.S. tour only hours before his scheduled departure on Wednesday. His office said he hoped to advance talks at a sensitive stage.

In an ominous note for the town that has long been a flashpoint of violence, troops preparing for the handover in Hebron staged a drill, closing off entrances so ambulances could evacuate make-believe casualties, Israel Television said.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat told reporters in Gaza on Thursday he was "not optimistic" an accord would be signed on Thursday. He said so far no progress had been made.
Palestinian officials said the sides were deadlocked over Israel's demand that its forces be allowed to enter PLO-run parts of Hebron in "hot pursuit" of suspected attackers.
"The Israeli side still insists on 'hot pursuit'. Therefore we could not agree," said Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas.
But Shomron said 'hot pursuit' was not the only problem that remained to be resolved. He did not elaborate.

Israel has completed many of the security arrangements to transfer the bulk of the twon to Palestinian police. But all of the Jews and 15,000 to 20,000 Arabs will remain under Israeli control in the centre of the town, military sources said.
The Palestinians are pushing for a written Israeli commitment to carry out further redeployments in West Bank rural areas promised by the previous government.
Netanyahu, a right-winger who in May ousted the centre-left government which signed the Hebron deal a year ago, wants to modify the accord aiming to bolster safeguards for the settlers.
But Hebron's Palestinians have a similar fear. U.S.-born Baruch Goldstein, a Jew from the adjacent Kiryat Arba settlement, massacred 29 Palestinians in Hebron in 1994.
